newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition threatens to quit parliaments.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition threatens to quit parliaments.

text.p: Opposition activists leading a wave of unrest threatened on Friday that their deputies would walk out of parliament and local councils unless "forged" election results were overturned.

One of the leaders of the Zajedno (Together) coalition Zoran Djindjic told tens of thousands of supporters at a rally in Belgrade his party would withdraw unless next Tuesday's session of the Serbian assembly refused to annul the local poll results.

One of the largest protests in a series of demonstrations over the last two weeks turned out in the Serbian capital, despite a public holiday and bitter weather, to express outrage at the official election results released earlier in the day.

The protests have jammed the city centre every day since the authorities stripped Zajedno of most victories in run-off local elections almost two weeks ago. Last Wednesday electoral commissions held a re-run of polling in disputed councils.
The state news agency Tanjug confirmed on Friday that Zajedno had retained control of some industrial towns including Kragujevac and Uzice.
But in Belgrade and Nis, where Zajedno had called for voters to boycott the re-runs, electoral authorities said President Slobodan Milosevic's ruling Socialist Party had won.
The results were greeted with derision by a crowd estimated at more than 80,000, joining what has become a daily ritual of defiance of Milosevic's rule.
The opposition and its supporters accuse the Socialists of massive electoral fraud and demand Milosevic's resignation.
"If they fail to annul the forged elections, we shall pull all our deputies out of both the federal and Serbian parliaments," said Djindjic.
The federal parliament represents rump Yugoslavia, which comprises only Serbia and tiny Montenegro.

"We don't recognize the re-run results in Belgrade and Nis," Djindjic told the crowd. "We are relinquishing those (local council) seats as well. We are not going to sit in the same benches with thieves."
Zajedno has said it will continue the demonstrations until its electoral victories are officially recognised.
One 28-year-old protester said she had joined the marches for the past four days and would continue for as long as the opposition organised them.
"I know this has very little chance of changing anything but what else can we do," she said. "We can no longer sit indoors and let Milosevic get away with his madness."
She insisted that growing international support was playing a key role in keeping the crowd motivated.
"If the world encourages us then we feel like we have a chance to achieve something," she said.
Diplomats said Milosevic, whose police force has kept a low profile, was betting the demonstration campaign across the country would eventually run out of steam.
Zajedno organisers acknowledged the protests had peaked but said they had dealt a blow to Milosevic's image abroad.
"We have torn off his mask in front of the world to show him as he really is -- a small-time Balkan dictator unable to bear the slightest defeat," Djindjic said.
